segment_name: The Grub Street Trap: Gissing's Opening Gambit

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something in our chat that stuck with me — that Gissing shows us Reardon's *circumstances* before he shows us the *man*. Can you take us right to the prose and show us what that actually looks like? What's Gissing doing at the sentence level that a less careful writer wouldn't do?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor reading aloud and making the formal argument viscerally — establish the prose-craft baseline before the others push back with sociology and psychology

questions.question: James, you've got a more combative read — you basically said the opening isn't tragic, it's *diagnostic*. That Gissing is showing us a machine that's working exactly as intended. Does that mean you think Eleanor's prose-craft argument is a distraction? Like, does it matter *how* beautifully Gissing writes about a trap if the trap itself is the point?
questions.intent: Provoke the structural-vs-formal disagreement directly — get James to go after the aesthetics-first reading and force Eleanor to defend whether craft and critique can coexist

questions.question: Caroline, you'd push back on both of them, I think. You said this opening works because it's *sensory* — you feel it before you understand it. But James is sitting here saying agency doesn't really matter, and Eleanor's talking about syntax. Where's the actual human being in this opening? Where's Reardon?
questions.intent: Draw out Caroline's character-and-interiority argument and set up the three-way tension between structural determinism, formal craft, and psychological specificity

questions.question: James, here's what I want to press you on — you compared Grub Street to 'freelance' in 2024. If Gissing's point is that the system hasn't changed, does that mean the novel is essentially a piece of journalism that's aged badly as fiction? Or is there something about the *literary form* — not just the argument — that keeps it alive?
questions.intent: Force James to either concede ground to Eleanor's formal argument or double down in a way that creates genuine friction — tests whether his sociological reading can account for why people still *feel* the novel

questions.question: Caroline, you mentioned Mrs. Reardon — and I don't think either James or Eleanor brought her up at all in our prep chats. Is the opening already doing something with her that we're missing if we only focus on Reardon and the market?
questions.intent: Introduce an underexplored angle that reframes the whole segment — if the trap has a gendered or domestic dimension from page one, that complicates both the economic-determinist and the prose-formalist readings

steering_notes: The core tension here is three-sided: James wants to talk about structure and systems, Eleanor wants to talk about prose craft and form, Caroline wants to talk about felt experience and character. These aren't incompatible but they'll *feel* incompatible on air, which is good. Let James and Eleanor go at it on the sociology-vs-craft question, then use Caroline to triangulate. If the conversation gets too abstract, push someone to read a specific passage — Eleanor and Caroline both want to, so give them the opening. Watch for the moment when James makes his 'freelance' contemporary comparison — that's a natural pivot point to ask the others whether the novel's form is what makes it more than journalism. The Mrs. Reardon thread is a good rescue move if the first four questions exhaust themselves early.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor argues Gissing withholds Reardon's interiority deliberately — Caroline directly contradicts this, saying the opening has 'devastating specificity' about him as a person. Get them to point at the same passage and disagree about what it's doing.

James says the system precedes any individual moral choice — Caroline says 'people make choices, even bad ones, and those choices matter morally.' This is the clearest direct contradiction in the pre-interviews and should be surfaced explicitly, ideally after Eleanor has laid out the formal argument so there's a third position in the room.

Eleanor and Caroline both want to quote Reardon's morning routine or study — let them both go at the same passage from different angles. That's the moment where the formal reading and the emotional reading can be tested against the same evidence.

segment_name: Reardon's Unravelling: Ambition, Failure, and the Writer's Fate

questions.question: James, you said something in our chat that I keep coming back to — that Reardon doesn't fail as a writer, the *system* fails him. But here's what I want to push on: the novel gives us this incredibly specific man, with this very particular temperament, this almost pathological fastidiousness. Does Gissing actually let us read this as a structural argument? Or does the specificity of Reardon as a *person* work against your case?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to articulate his strongest systemic reading, then leave space for Hartley and Woodcourt to challenge the 'victim of capitalism' framing with the personality argument

questions.question: Eleanor, you've been looking at the prose itself — the sentences, the syntax — as a kind of clinical instrument Gissing uses to track Reardon's collapse. Can you walk us through what you mean by that? Because I think there's something almost perverse about what you're describing — a style that gets *worse* as the man gets worse, but it's still beautiful?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read or paraphrase a specific passage showing formal deterioration — the gap between conception and execution — and provoke Blackstone to respond on whether form or economics is doing the heavier lifting

questions.question: Caroline, you mentioned that this novel is actually funnier than people admit — and I have to say that surprised me. Because when I think of Reardon I think of this grey, exhausted man staring at blank pages. Where is the dark comedy you're seeing, and does it change what the novel is *doing* to us emotionally?
questions.intent: Draw out Woodcourt's tenderness-plus-gallows-humor reading, which complements but also quietly challenges Hartley's clinical framing and Blackstone's furious sociological one — create a three-way tension between rage, precision, and dark warmth

questions.question: Eleanor, James just argued — or will argue — that Reardon's predicament has nothing to do with talent and everything to do with capital. But you said something to me about how Reardon's own temperament becomes part of the machinery of his destruction. So which is it — is this a novel about what the market does to writers, or about what a certain kind of writer does to himself?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between the structural reading and the psychological one — this is the core disagreement of the segment and shouldn't be smoothed over

questions.question: Here's the thing that gets me about the ending — and Caroline, I want to put this to you because you said the ending is unbearable rather than just depressing. Gissing doesn't give us a grand tragic scene. It's almost undramatic. Why does *that* work, when a more melodramatic death might have made the same point more loudly?
questions.intent: Close the segment on Gissing's formal restraint and the question of whether the novel earns its emotional impact — gets all three talking about what literary generosity actually looks like and whether the refusal to sentimentalize is Gissing's greatest or most cold-blooded move

steering_notes: The live disagreement to chase in this segment is the one between structural determinism (Blackstone) and psychological interiority (Hartley and Woodcourt, who agree more than they'd admit). Don't let anyone settle into the comfortable 'it's both' answer — keep pressing the 'which one is the novel actually *arguing*' question. Woodcourt's humour angle is the wild card that can crack open any moment the conversation gets too solemn or too theoretical. Let her use it. If Blackstone gets too academic, redirect to a specific passage. The goal is to end the segment with listeners feeling the weight of Reardon's fate without having been told how to feel about it.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that Reardon's failure is structural directly contradicts Hartley's view that his temperament is 'part of the machinery' — this needs to be surfaced explicitly and not mediated too quickly

Hartley's reading of stylistic deterioration as the novel's real horror complements but complicates Woodcourt's claim that the prose remains generous and beautiful throughout — they're describing the same sentences and possibly reaching opposite conclusions
Woodcourt's insistence on staying with the *feeling* of the pages is a methodological challenge to Blackstone's social history framing — worth naming that tension openly rather than letting it simmer

All three agree that Gissing refuses sentimentality, but they mean very different things by that — Blackstone means political refusal, Hartley means formal restraint, Woodcourt means literary generosity. That three-way split on one shared claim is worth a direct moment of comparison

segment_name: The Market Made Flesh: How Milvain Learns to Thrive

questions.question: Eleanor, you made this observation in our pre-chat that really stuck with me — you said that Milvain doesn't *choose* to think like a market creature, he just gradually *loses access* to any other way of thinking. Can you point us to a specific passage where you can actually hear that happening in the prose itself?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read a passage showing the colonization of Milvain's interiority by market language — ideally the free indirect discourse with commercial jargon — and establish her structural-formal argument early so Blackstone and Woodcourt can respond to it

questions.question: James, I want to push you on something. Eleanor's just shown us how the *prose* is doing this — the sentences themselves going shallow as Milvain succeeds. But your argument is essentially that we shouldn't judge him at all, that the market made this inevitable. Doesn't that let Milvain off the hook in a way that Gissing himself doesn't seem willing to?
questions.intent: Create productive friction between Blackstone's economic determinism and Hartley's formal critique — Blackstone wants to exonerate Milvain structurally, Hartley shows the prose *does* indict him, this tension should be rich

questions.question: Caroline, there's a moment you mentioned — where Milvain watches someone else's desperation and feels relief. That feels like the darkest thing in the novel to me. Can you read us that passage? Because I think that's where your argument about complicity really lands — Gissing is making *us* feel that relief too, isn't he?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read the passage about Milvain observing another's desperation, and push her to articulate how the prose makes readers complicit — this should land as the emotional gut-punch of the segment

questions.question: James, let me steelman the other side for a second. Both Eleanor and Caroline are essentially saying: yes, the system is the villain, but Gissing still shows us Milvain *diminishing* as a person — there's loss in his wins. Does your economic reading have room for that? Can you hold both — the system is responsible *and* something real is being destroyed in him?
questions.intent: Push Blackstone to either synthesize with Hartley and Woodcourt or sharpen his disagreement — forces him to address whether his structural argument can account for the affective, moral dimension both other experts feel in the novel

questions.question: Caroline, you said something that I keep coming back to — that Gissing's portrait of how markets corrupt *language* is still the most accurate account we have, that it's prophetic rather than dated. So let's go there. When you read the passages where Milvain's internal voice goes slick and glib — what contemporary writer, what contemporary moment, does it make you think of?
questions.intent: Open the novel outward to the present — Woodcourt's 'prophetic' claim should be tested against the contemporary literary market, likely provoking Blackstone on historicization and Hartley on whether form travels across periods

steering_notes: The big tension to manage: Blackstone wants to exonerate Milvain via economic necessity, Hartley wants to show the prose structurally indicts him regardless of intention, and Woodcourt holds both but insists on tragedy over sociology. Don't let Blackstone's historicism become a lecture — keep redirecting to specific passages and moments. The sweet spot is the third question onward, when all three are responding to each other rather than presenting their own positions. Push hard on the complicity point — all three experts circle it but none named it as their central claim, and it may be the most interesting place the conversation can go. If energy flags, ask whose side they'd want Milvain on if he reviewed their own work.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's formal argument (prose goes shallow as Milvain succeeds) directly challenges Blackstone's exoneration thesis — Blackstone says the system eliminates all alternatives, but Hartley's reading suggests Gissing's own narrative voice is quietly condemning Milvain even while documenting his rationality; get them to address this head-on

Woodcourt's 'domestication not destruction' claim complements Hartley's structural argument but arrives from a different direction — Hartley sees it in sentence-level form, Woodcourt sees it in character arc; they should be encouraged to build on each other rather than repeat separately

Blackstone's insistence that 'morality becomes a luxury good' is a direct provocation to Woodcourt's tragic reading — Woodcourt thinks Milvain *had* a choice and made the wrong one; Blackstone thinks the choice was always illusory. This is the sharpest disagreement in the room and should be surfaced explicitly, ideally around the passage where Milvain calculates his principles against his prospects

questions.question: Caroline, you mentioned something in our chat that stuck with me — this idea that you can *feel* Marian's imprisonment in the rhythm of the sentences themselves, not just in what happens to her. Can you take us into that? Like, what does Gissing actually do on the page that makes the prose itself feel like a cage?
questions.intent: Open the segment with the most visceral, sensory entry point — get Caroline to read a passage contrasting Marian's internal pace vs. her performed speech, hook listeners emotionally before the structural arguments land

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to push on something. You said Gissing almost *refuses* to give Marian a full interior monologue — the way he does for Jasper, say. But Caroline just described this racing inner life in the syntax. So which is it — is Gissing letting us in, or keeping us out? And does that distinction actually matter for how we read her?
questions.intent: Create productive friction between Eleanor and Caroline on the question of narrative access — Eleanor's 'formal distance as entrapment' vs. Caroline's 'syntax as emotional truth' — get Eleanor to name the specific formal choice and ideally quote the fog passage or a reading scene

questions.question: James, you're going to push back on both of them, I suspect. Because from what you told me, the real story isn't about Gissing's craft or even Marian's inner life — it's about what the law actually permitted her to do in 1891. So I want to ask you directly: does it matter that she's *brilliant*? Would a less intelligent Marian have fared any differently?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to make his sharpest structural argument — that intellect is irrelevant when the institution is designed to exclude — and provoke Eleanor and Caroline who both centre Marian's intelligence as the key to the tragedy

questions.question: Eleanor, James is essentially saying Marian's tragedy is impersonal — she's a case study in structural violence, not a person making meaningful choices. But you said something really provocative to me: that Marian *chooses* her constraints, and that's what makes it more devastating, not less. Can you defend that? Because it sounds almost like you're blaming her.
questions.intent: Force Eleanor to articulate her most uncomfortable argument — that Marian internalises and participates in her own imprisonment — which should provoke strong reactions from both Caroline (who wants to protect Marian's dignity) and Blackstone (who sees no meaningful choice under those legal conditions)

questions.question: Caroline, last one — and I want you to be honest here. There's a version of this conversation where we've spent the whole time talking *about* Marian with a kind of tender, protective sympathy. And I wonder if that's exactly the trap Gissing is setting. Is the way we *discuss* her part of the problem — are we doing to Marian what Victorian society did, making her the object of the story rather than the subject?
questions.intent: Meta-level provocation to close the segment — push Caroline to either defend emotional engagement as legitimate response or acknowledge the irony of the panel's own dynamic, potentially drawing in Eleanor's complicity argument and Blackstone's refusal of redemptive framing

steering_notes: Open emotionally through Caroline, then let Eleanor introduce formal/craft tension, then bring Blackstone in as the structural cold water. The risk is that Blackstone's legal-historical argument, while strong, can drain the air from the room — use it as provocation, not conclusion. Keep pulling the conversation back to specific passages; all three experts have text they want to read and the segment needs those moments to breathe. The final question is designed to make the panel slightly uncomfortable in a productive way — lean into any awkward pause there.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor's claim that Marian actively chooses her constraints directly contradicts Blackstone's position that choice is structurally foreclosed — this is the segment's richest disagreement and should be drawn out explicitly around Q3-Q4

Caroline's reading of Gissing's syntax as giving us Marian's inner life sits in tension with Eleanor's argument that the formal distance is the point — ask them to look at the same passage and describe what they see
Blackstone's line that a male Marian would simply be Jasper Milvain is a grenade — throw it early enough that Eleanor and Caroline can respond across multiple questions, not just once

All three experts resist sentimentality but from different directions: Eleanor via formal analysis, Blackstone via structural critique, Caroline via insistence on dignity over pity — surfacing this three-way disagreement about *how* to resist sentimentality could be the segment's most surprising moment

segment_name: Grub Street's Social Machine: Class, Commerce, and Literary Culture

questions.question: James, you've called this novel 'functionally a legal document' — an indictment of contracts and copyright loopholes as much as a work of fiction. But here's what I want to push on: does reading it that way risk flattening something? Like, is there a version of your argument where you're basically extracting the economic history and leaving the novel behind?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to defend his materialist reading at its sharpest, and set up Hartley to challenge whether form and content can be separated the way he implies

questions.question: Eleanor, I want you to actually read us something — pick a passage where you think Gissing's sentence structure is doing the heavy lifting, where the *form* is the argument. Because I think some listeners are going to hear James and think: okay, economic critique, got it. What am I missing if I read this purely for content?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to quote directly and make the case for formal reading — ideally a word-counting or editorial negotiation scene — so the passage is in the room and both other experts have to respond to it

questions.question: Caroline, you've said Marian Yule should be read as the novel's true protagonist — and honestly that's a provocation, because she's not the character most readers remember first. Make the case. Why does she matter more than Reardon to what Gissing is actually arguing?
questions.intent: Draw out the Marian argument in full, which directly challenges both Blackstone's systemic reading (she's an individual moral case) and implicitly provokes Hartley on the question of interiority and character agency

questions.question: You've said the prose itself grows labored when characters are broke — that the sentences mirror the deprivation. Eleanor's making a similar point about form, but I think you two are actually saying slightly different things. Caroline, do you and Eleanor agree on this, or is there a real disagreement hiding underneath the surface?
questions.intent: Force a productive clarification or open conflict between Woodcourt and Hartley — Woodcourt sees style as mirroring psychological exhaustion, Hartley sees it as formal argument about capitalism; these are not the same claim

questions.question: James, you've said we should feel *anger* reading this, not just sympathy — that the Victorian pathos reading is too soft. But Caroline's just argued that Marian's tragedy is almost too bleak for anger, that the novel is genuinely pessimistic about whether resistance is even possible. Can anger be the right response to a novel that doesn't believe escape is on the table?
questions.intent: Create a direct clash between Blackstone's activist, structural anger and Woodcourt's bleaker psychological pessimism — and invite Hartley to weigh in on whether Gissing's formal choices imply any hope at all

steering_notes: The big tension to keep live throughout: is Grub Street a *system* you can analyze and be angry at (Blackstone), a *psychological trap* you feel in the prose (Woodcourt), or a *formal argument* embedded in the novel's structure itself (Hartley)? These three readings don't fully overlap and the best moments will come when experts realize they're talking about slightly different things. Don't let anyone settle into pure agreement — Woodcourt and Hartley sound similar on style but have real differences on interiority and agency. Push that. Keep passages in the room: if someone quotes something, make the other two respond to the same lines before moving on.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone says the tragedy is structural not moral — Woodcourt says the system is *irrational*, not a coherent machine. That's a direct contradiction worth surfacing: can you be angry at a system if it doesn't even have a logic?

Hartley argues Gissing *limits* interiority deliberately as a formal choice — Woodcourt argues Marian's interiority is the novel's sharpest tool. These can't both be fully true. Get them to locate where they diverge.

Blackstone wants to resist pathos — but Woodcourt's Marian reading IS pathos, just very dark pathos. Ask Blackstone directly whether Marian's story is the kind of thing he wants readers to feel or to analyze.

All three agree style matters — but for different reasons. Hartley: style as argument. Woodcourt: style as affect. Blackstone implicitly: style as evidence. A single quoted passage could expose all three positions simultaneously if handled right.

segment_name: The Comedy of Desperation: Gissing's Satirical Eye

questions.question: Eleanor, you used this phrase in our pre-conversation that I keep coming back to — 'narrative schadenfreude.' You said the reader feels superior to these characters, and then Gissing yanks that comfort away. Can you find us a passage where you actually hear that trap being set? Where does Gissing do that most surgically?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read a specific passage demonstrating the architectural irony, and establish her 'no authorial wink' thesis as the baseline for the segment

questions.question: Caroline, I want to push on something — because Eleanor is basically saying the comedy is structural, architectural, built into the form. But your instinct is that Gissing is also just... having fun with language. That there's verbal pleasure here, a dark waltz you called it. Are those two things compatible, or is one of you describing a different book?
questions.intent: Force a direct comparison between Caroline's 'verbal music' thesis and Eleanor's 'architectural irony' thesis — sounds like agreement on the surface but may crack open under pressure

questions.question: James, I have to put this to you directly, because you said something in our chat that I think is going to annoy both Caroline and Eleanor — you said the desperation in this novel isn't comedy at all, it's documentary horror that's been dressed up to be publishable. So are they both wrong? Is the 'comedy' just a survival strategy Gissing adopted to get the book into print?
questions.intent: Provoke direct disagreement by having Blackstone challenge the comic framing entirely, forcing Caroline and Eleanor to defend their readings

questions.question: Okay but James — find me the passage. You said Gissing is showing us characters who follow the rules and still fail catastrophically. Where's that moment in the text, and when you read it out loud, does it actually sound like horror to you, or does it sound like something else?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to read a passage aloud and test whether his 'documentary horror' framing survives contact with the actual prose — the reading itself may contradict his thesis

questions.question: Caroline, you said the real scandal is that Gissing shows characters becoming complicit in their own degradation — and you called it tragedy wearing a smile. Eleanor said almost the same thing but landed somewhere different: she says Gissing never separates himself morally from his characters, he's inside the machinery with them. Is there a difference there, or have you two just described the same thing from opposite ends?
questions.intent: Create a moment of synthesis or productive tension between Caroline and Eleanor's strongest takes, and push toward the question of authorial position — is Gissing laughing at his characters or with them

steering_notes: The central fault line is whether the comedy in New Grub Street is a formal/aesthetic phenomenon (Caroline and Eleanor, broadly) or a political camouflage strategy (Blackstone). Let that tension run. Don't resolve it too early. The most productive disagreement will be around authorial complicity — all three have views on whether Gissing is inside or outside the machinery, and they don't actually agree as much as they think they do. Push for passages read aloud whenever possible; the prose itself will do a lot of the arguing. Watch for Caroline and Eleanor to seem like they're agreeing when they're actually describing different things — surface consensus, underlying divergence.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor's 'no authorial wink' thesis vs. Caroline's 'cruel tenderness' — Caroline implies Gissing does signal his sympathy through prose style, which Eleanor's architectural model seems to deny; worth surfacing directly

Blackstone's claim that 'the desperation isn't comedy' is a direct challenge to both other experts' central premises — he should be asked to respond to a specific passage one of them has just read, not just assert the thesis abstractly

All three experts independently landed on some version of 'reader complicity' but with completely different implications: for Eleanor it's about self-deception, for Blackstone it's about economic beneficiary guilt, for Caroline it's about aesthetic recognition. That three-way collision is the richest moment in the segment if it can be engineered.

segment_name: No Exit: Synthesis and the Tragedy of Compromise

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our pre-interview that stopped me cold — that death would actually be cleaner than what Gissing does to his characters. That survival is the real punishment. Can you unpack that? Because most tragedy gives us a fall. What's Gissing doing that's different?
questions.intent: Open the segment with Woodcourt's most provocative thesis — that surviving failure is worse than dramatic collapse — and let it hang in the air for the others to react to

questions.question: James, I want to push you on something. Caroline is describing this as an interior experience — the moment someone watches themselves shrink and accepts it. You've been pretty firm that this is about institutions, not psychology. But aren't those the same thing? Doesn't the institution get inside the person? Where exactly do you draw that line?
questions.intent: Force Blackstone to either defend or nuance his systems-versus-psychology position directly against Woodcourt's framing, setting up genuine friction

questions.question: Eleanor, you made a claim that I find either brilliant or slightly mad, and I genuinely can't decide which: that Gissing writes *like* hack work in places, deliberately, as a formal argument. If that's true, can you show us exactly where? Give us the passage — what does a sentence that's intentionally compromising itself actually look like on the page?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read aloud and close-read a specific passage where she argues Gissing enacts formal compromise — creates a concrete, textual anchor for an otherwise abstract claim

questions.question: James, Hartley is saying the tragedy lives at the sentence level — in prose choices. You've been arguing it lives in the statute books, in bankruptcy law, in the absence of copyright protection. Is there any version of this novel where you'd say the individual psychology actually matters? Or is that just the wrong question to be asking?
questions.intent: Provoke Blackstone into either conceding ground to the literary-formal argument or doubling down in a way that Hartley and Woodcourt will want to immediately contest

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you on this. Caroline, you said readers catastrophically underestimate Marian and Amy — that they're trapped by economics, not weakness. But James would say *everyone* in this novel is trapped by economics. So what's specifically gendered about their trap? And Eleanor, I'm curious whether you think Gissing's prose treats them differently at the sentence level — does his style change when he's inside their heads?
questions.intent: Close the segment by triangulating all three experts around gender, economics, and form — Woodcourt on social reading, Blackstone on structural argument, Hartley on prose texture — creating a genuine three-way synthesis moment

steering_notes: The central tension to keep live throughout is the three-way pull between form (Hartley), interior psychology (Woodcourt), and institutional structure (Blackstone). Don't let any one frame dominate too early. The most productive friction is Blackstone versus Woodcourt on whether compromise is chosen or coerced — Hartley's formal argument can actually mediate that fight, because she's saying the prose itself enacts the absence of genuine choice. Push toward that triangulation by the final question. Keep Blackstone honest — he can slide into abstraction; bring him back to the text. Keep Hartley from getting too technical about prose mechanics without grounding it in a passage. Woodcourt is the emotional anchor; let her have the last word if the conversation allows it.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's 'forced moves in a rigged game' framing directly contradicts Woodcourt's interest in the interior moment of self-betrayal — both can be true, and getting them to argue about whether it matters which it is will be electric

Hartley's claim that Gissing writes 'like hack work in places' is a formal version of Blackstone's institutional argument — he may not realize they're compatible, and pointing that out should produce a productive surprise

Woodcourt's observation that Gissing's syntax becomes 'shorter, choppier, more defeated' as characters lose hope is something Hartley will want to engage with closely — they're both doing close formal reading but from different angles, and they may not have realized how much they agree

Blackstone's dismissal of romanticized artistic struggle should be aimed directly at Hartley's language about 'the romance of noble suffering' — she preemptively pushes back on this, which means there's a real argument waiting to happen there if it's surfaced
